p2.key:
Kc = [NO2]2 / [N2O4]

Square brackets (concentrations) are required.

(i) Yield of NO2 increases: adding N2O4 shifts the equilibrium to the right (Kc is constant, so [NO2] must rise).

(ii) Yield decreases: higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (1 mol N2O4 vs 2 mol NO2), so equilibrium shifts left.

(iii) No change: a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

(i) 0.2 mol N2O4 reacted, giving 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 mol NO2.

(ii) Volume is 1.00 dm3, so Kc = (0.4)2/0.8 = 0.2 mol dm−3

Units: (mol dm−3)2/(mol dm−3) = mol dm−3.

Kc increases, because the forward reaction is endothermic: raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (in the endothermic direction).

Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of K.

(i) Dynamic equilibrium: the forward and reverse reactions continue but at equal rates, so concentrations remain constant.

(ii) Homogeneous equilibrium: all reactants and products are in the same phase.

(iii) Closed system: no exchange of matter with the surroundings. (The 1999 scheme said “matter or energy”; today a closed system can exchange energy but not matter — an isolated system exchanges neither.)

p2.key:
Kc = [NH3]2 / ([H2]3[N2])

Units: (mol dm−3)2/(mol dm−3)4 = mol−2 dm6

(i) Increasing volume: Kc unchanged for both (K depends only on temperature). HI: no change in position, since 2 mol gas → 2 mol gas. NH3: shifts left (less NH3), because the side with more gas molecules (4 vs 2) is favoured at lower pressure.

(ii) Lowering temperature: HI (ΔH = +52, endothermic forward): shifts left (more H2, I2) and Kc decreases. NH3 (ΔH = −92, exothermic forward): shifts right (more NH3) and Kc increases.

(iii) Adding a catalyst: no effect on position or on Kc for either; it speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster.

The reaction HI ⇌ ½H2 + ½I2 is the reverse of the formation reaction, halved.

Reversing gives 1/K; halving the coefficients gives the square root: K = √(1/54.7) = 0.135

(i) The forward reaction is endothermic: heat is absorbed (products have higher enthalpy than reactants).

(ii) Kc decreases: lowering the temperature favours the exothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium shifts left.

(iii) At equilibrium: [N2] = [O2] = 1.6 − x, [NO] = 2x
Kc = [NO]2/([N2][O2]) = (2x)2/(1.6 − x)2 = 1.7 × 10−3
Square root: 2x/(1.6 − x) = 0.0412 → x = 0.0323
[NO] = 2x = 0.065 mol dm−3

(Using 1.6 instead of 1.6 − x gives 0.066 and scores 2/3 unless the approximation is stated.)

(i) The temperature increases — the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −91 kJ mol−1).

(ii) [CH3OH] increases: lowering temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, shifting the equilibrium to the right.

(i) Kc = [CH3OH] / ([CO][H2]2); units mol−2 dm6 (units needed for the mark).

(ii) 85 % yield: 0.85 mol CH3OH forms; CO left = 1.00 − 0.85 = 0.15 mol; H2 left = 2.00 − 1.70 = 0.30 mol. Total volume 450 cm3 = 0.450 dm3.
[CO] = 0.333, [H2] = 0.667, [CH3OH] = 1.889 mol dm−3
Kc = 1.889 / (0.333 × 0.6672) = 12.8 mol−2 dm6

(iii) e.g. a higher temperature is used for a faster rate (which lowers the equilibrium yield); or the system is not allowed to reach equilibrium (product removed early); side reactions; leaks.

(iv) No effect on Kc: a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally.

(i) Any two: reversible reaction; rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction; no net change in concentrations of reactants and products; closed system.

(ii) Kc = [CH3COOC2H5][H2O] / ([CH3COOH][C2H5OH])

(iii) At equilibrium: acid = ethanol = 1.0 − 0.67 = 0.33 mol; ester = water = 0.67 mol. Volume cancels (equal moles top and bottom).

Kc = (0.67 × 0.67)/(0.33 × 0.33) = 4.1 (accept 4.0).

Kw increases as temperature rises (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ → 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴), so [H⁺] and [OH⁻] increase.

The equilibrium therefore shifts to the right on heating.

By Le Châtelier, raising T favours the endothermic direction, so the dissociation of water is endothermic.

(i) No effect on the position of equilibrium: a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is only reached faster.

(ii) No effect: at constant volume the amounts and concentrations (partial pressures) of N2, H2 and NH3 are unchanged, so Q still equals K. (Helium does not take part in the reaction.)

Kc = [H2(g)][CO(g)] / [H2O(g)] (C(s) is a solid and is omitted).

Units: (mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³)/(mol dm⁻³) = mol dm⁻³. (Units of K are not required in the 2025 course.)

The forward reaction is endothermic, because Kc increases as temperature increases (forward reaction favoured by heating).

(i) Rate of forward reaction

  • ↑ Temperature: rate increases – a greater proportion of collisions have E ≥ Ea (main reason; not just 'more collisions').
  • ↑ Pressure: rate increases – higher concentration of H2O(g), so more frequent collisions.
  • ↑ Surface area of C: rate increases – more exposed carbon, more frequent collisions.

(ii) [H2O] : [H2] ratio

  • ↑ T: ratio decreases – the endothermic forward reaction is favoured, absorbing the added heat.
  • ↑ P: ratio increases – equilibrium shifts left, to the side with fewer gas moles (1 mol vs 2 mol).
  • ↑ Surface area: no effect – the solid's 'concentration' is constant, equilibrium position unchanged.

(iii) Kc: ↑ T increases Kc (endothermic); pressure and surface area have no effect – K depends only on temperature.

Diagram: energy vs reaction coordinate with products above reactants (endothermic), an Ea hump, and a lower hump for the catalysed path.

The catalyst increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions (equally, as Ea is lowered for both).

The position of equilibrium is unchanged; equilibrium is just reached faster.

2HI(g) ⇌ H2(g) + I2(g)

One mark for the correct equation with ⇌ (dissociation direction), one for state symbols (all gases at 440 °C).

(i) Kc = [H2][I2] / [HI]²; no units (they cancel).

(ii) HI reacted = 1.00 − 0.78 = 0.22 mol, so H2 = I2 = 0.11 mol (1.0 dm³, so these are concentrations).

Kc = (0.11 × 0.11)/(0.78)² = 0.0121/0.608 = 0.020

Kc increases from 0.020 (440 °C) to 0.04 (600 °C), so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (favours products).

Heating favours the endothermic direction, so the dissociation is endothermic.

(i) No change: there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 ⇌ 2).

(ii) Equilibrium shifts to the right: the system reduces the added HI by dissociating it (Le Châtelier).

(iii) No change: a catalyst increases the forward and reverse rates equally; equilibrium is just reached faster.
Their Kc values are much smaller than that of HI, so HCl and HBr are dissociated to a much smaller extent (equilibrium lies far to the left; HCl least of all).

Sketch rate vs time: forward curve starts high and falls; reverse starts at zero and rises; the two curves meet and become horizontal (equal and constant) [2].

Forward: reactant concentrations are highest at the start so rate is high; as they are used up the rate decreases [2].
Reverse: no products at t = 0 so rate is zero; rate increases as product concentrations build up [2].
Equilibrium is reached when forward rate = reverse rate (dynamic, concentrations constant) [1].

The reaction is endothermic [1]: Kc increases from 1.1 to 4.9 as temperature rises [1], so higher T shifts equilibrium to the right — by Le Châtelier the forward reaction absorbs the added heat, so it must be endothermic [1].

Kc decreases [1], because the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative): raising T favours the endothermic reverse reaction, moving equilibrium to the left [1].
The mixture becomes darker (more brown) [1]. Lower pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with more gas molecules — left (2 mol NO2 vs 1 mol N2O4) — producing more brown NO2 [1].

(i) No effect – equal numbers of gas moles (2) on each side.

(ii) Shifts to the right – the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +52 kJ), so it absorbs the added heat.

(iii) No effect – a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally; equilibrium is just reached faster.

(i) Experiment 1: [I2] = 0.01, so [H2] = 0.01; HI used = 2 × 0.01 = 0.02 → [HI] = 0.06 − 0.02 = 0.04 mol dm−3.
Kc = (0.01)(0.01)/(0.04)2 = 0.0625 (6.25 × 10−2)

Kc = (0.02)(0.02)/(0.04)2 = 0.25

(ii) Experiment 2: Kc is larger, so equilibrium lies further right; for an endothermic forward reaction K increases with temperature.
Kc = [SO3]2 / ([SO2]2[O2])

(i) Vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5.

(ii) The catalyst has no effect on Kc: it increases forward and reverse rates equally. It increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so equilibrium is reached faster.

(i) Shifts to the right (products): the system reduces pressure by favouring the side with fewer gas moles (3 → 2).

(ii) Shifts to the right: to replace (compensate for) the SO3 removed.
Exothermic: Kc decreases as temperature increases, so higher temperature favours the reverse reaction, meaning the forward reaction releases heat.

Equilibrium: SO2 = 1.00 mol, O2 = 1.75 mol, SO3 = 0.500 mol

Concentrations (÷ 1.50 dm3): [SO2] = 0.667, [O2] = 1.17, [SO3] = 0.333 mol dm−3

Kc = (0.333)2 / [(0.667)2(1.17)] = 0.214 dm3 mol−1 (0.213 accepted)

Kc = [H2]3[CO] / ([CH4][H2O]). The balanced equation is CH4 + H2O ⇌ 3H2 + CO.

(i) Higher T: the forward reaction is endothermic, so equilibrium shifts to the right and Kc increases.

(ii) Higher pressure: equilibrium shifts to the left (2 mol gas on the left, 4 on the right). Kc does not change, because only temperature changes K.

(i) 1.6 mol of CO and of H2O reacted, so CO = 2.0 − 1.6 = 0.4 mol and H2O = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6 mol.
Kc = (1.6 × 1.6)/(0.4 × 1.6) = 4.0. Volume cancels because the moles of gas are equal on both sides.

(ii) Let x react: x2/(2.0 − x)2 = 4 → x/(2.0 − x) = 2 → x = 1.33.
H2 = CO2 = 1.33 mol; CO = H2O = 0.67 mol. With Kc = 9.0 you get 1.5 and 0.5.

• A catalyst has no effect on the position of equilibrium.
  • It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally (it lowers Ea for both), so equilibrium is reached faster but its extent is unchanged.
  • It has no effect on Kc.
  • The equilibrium concentrations are unchanged, because Kc changes only with temperature.

(i) The equilibrium shifts to the right, to use up the added Br−.

(ii) It shifts to the left, because OH− neutralizes and removes H+, so the system replaces it.

(iii) No effect on the position. The catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally (it lowers Ea for both).

K decreases. The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction.
The red-brown colour intensifies (becomes darker). The added H+ shifts the equilibrium to the right to use it up, which produces more Br2.

(i) CH4(g) + 2H2O(g) ⇌ 4H2(g) + CO2(g)
Kc = [H2]4[CO2] / ([CH4][H2O]2); units mol2 dm−6.

(ii) High temperature: the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts right to absorb the heat. Low pressure: the right-hand side has more gas moles (5 vs 3), so the equilibrium shifts right. “Because of Le Chatelier” alone scores nothing.

(iii) At high pressure the gas concentrations are greater, so collisions are more frequent and the rate is faster. This is a compromise with yield.

(ii) [NO] decreases. The forward reaction is exothermic, so higher T favours the reverse (endothermic) reaction.

(iii) No effect. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is only reached faster.

p2.key: Only the increase in temperature changes Kc. Kc decreases, because the forward reaction is exothermic. Pressure and catalysts do not change K.

• Increasing temperature: the equilibrium shifts left, in the endothermic direction, to absorb the added heat (the forward reaction is exothermic).
  • Increasing pressure: the equilibrium shifts right, towards fewer gas moles (1 mol of gas on the left, 0 on the right), to reduce the pressure.

  • H2 = 1.5 mol

(ii) Kc = [CO][H2]3 / ([CH4][H2O])

Kc = 7.65 × 10−4 / (7.84 × 10−3)2 = 12.5

(iii) Lower temperature: Kc increases and [SO2Cl2] increases, because the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −84.5 kJ) and is favoured by a decrease in temperature.

(iv) Kc unchanged (depends only on temperature). [SO2Cl2] decreases: the larger volume (lower pressure) favours the reverse reaction, which has more moles of gas (2 vs 1).

(v) No effect on [SO2Cl2]: a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally (lowers both activation energies), so the position of equilibrium does not change.

  • Macroscopic properties (e.g. concentrations, pressure, colour) remain constant (in a closed system).

[N2] = 0.20 − 0.030 = 0.17 mol dm−3; [H2] = 0.20 − 0.090 = 0.11 mol dm−3.
Kc = (0.060)2 / (0.17 × 0.113) = 16.
